newsitem.title: USA: US lawmakers unveil securities lawsuits proposals.
newsitem.headline: US lawmakers unveil securities lawsuits proposals.

text.p: U.S. lawmakers unveiled bipartisan legislation on Wednesday that would stop securities class action lawsuits that are traditionally filed in federal courts from migrating to state courts.
California Democrat Rep. Anna Eshoo and Washington Republican Rep. Rick White, who introduced the bill, said it would give investors more information and safeguard growing companies.

"This bill will finish the job we started in Congress to give investors more information and growing companies more opportunities to invest in the economy -- not meritless lawsuits," White said at press briefing.

In December 1995, Congress passed the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, over a presidental veto, which sought to reduce the number of meritless cases in federal courts by raising qualifying standards.
That bill was designed to provide relief to companies from such lawsuits, but lawmakers have said a federal preemption over state jurisdiction in those cases is needed.

"The passage of such standards for lawsuits involving nationally traded securities would ensure that federal securities laws are not undermined," the Securities Industry Association said in support of the Eshoo-White bill.

"If states continue to allow trial lawyers to file meritless cases rightfully shut out of federal courts, companies will not be relieved of onerous legal costs," SIA chairman Marc Lackritz said in a statement.

The Government Finance Officers Association, which opposes the bill, said it "considers any preemption legislation which sets a national standard for states comparable to that of the federal law to be an extension of bad law."
GFOA, representing state and local public officials, said in a statement it "will continue to oppose efforts to preempt the rights of states to protect state and local government."
The Software Publishers Association hailed the new legislation saying it will close a "gaping loophole" in the reform act "exploited by law firms specializing in frivolous lawsuits."

"Securities lawyers should not be able to gain an advantage by choosing the court in which to file their cases and to have that choice make a difference in the outcome of the case," SPA's Mark Nebergall said in a statement.
